Temporal Power
tem´po-ral pow´er
n. phrase (civil or political rule, as distinct from the spiritual; and, in controversy, the papal claim to wield both swords)
Latin temporalis, of time, from tempus, time. Webster already pairs the senses: temporal as opposed to spiritual, and temporal power as secular, civil, or political power. The papal claim is that the church's head holds that sword as well as the spiritual one.

Biblical Definition

Temporal power is rule in this world: courts, swords, taxes, the things that belong to time. Christ drew the line with a sentence that still judges Rome: “My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight” (John 18:36). He would not be made a king by force: “When Jesus therefore perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone” (John 6:15). He refused the divider's bench: “Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?” (Luk 12:14). And He left Caesar his own: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's” (Mat 22:21). The apostle's soldier is not entangled: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life” (2Ti 2:4). The civil magistrate is a real ordinance of God. That is not the pope's claim. The pope's claim is that the Vicar of Christ holds both swords, and may depose princes. The New Testament never gives that office to any apostle, still less to a later Roman bishop.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines temporal as pertaining to this life or this world or the body only; secular; opposed to spiritual, and also opposed to ecclesiastical; as temporal power, that is, secular, civil or political power.

expand to see more

TEM'PORAL, a. [L. temporalis, from tempus, time.]

1. Pertaining to this life or this world or the body only; secular; as temporal concerns; temporal affairs. In this sense, it is opposed to spiritual.

In this sense also it is opposed to ecclesiastical; as temporal power, that is, secular, civil or political power; temporal courts, those which take cognizance of civil suits.

Temporal jurisdiction is that which regards civil and political affairs.

2. Measured or limited by time, or by this life or this state of things; having limited existence; opposed to eternal.

Key Scripture

John 18:36 — "Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now is my kingdom not from hence."

Mat 22:21 — "They say unto him, Caesar's. Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's."

John 6:15 — "When Jesus therefore perceived that they would come and take him by force, to make him a king, he departed again into a mountain himself alone."

Luk 12:14 — "And he said unto him, Man, who made me a judge or a divider over you?"

2Ti 2:4 — "No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier."

Modern Corruption

Rome made the two swords one, and some Protestants then emptied the magistrate of any duty under God at all.

expand to see more

Unam Sanctam (1302) is the classic papal sentence: two swords, both the pope's, the spiritual to be used by the church and the temporal to be used for the church. John 18:36 will not wear it. If the kingdom were of this world, the servants would fight. They did not. Peter was told to put up the sword. A see that deposes kings and raises armies in Peter's name has already answered Jesus with a no.

The opposite Protestant error is to hear “not of this world” as if Caesar were a neutral zone where God's law has no claim. The dictionary's magistrate is a minister of God, a real ordinance, owed honour in all things lawful. Temporal power belongs to that office, not to the bishop of Rome, and not to a church that has forgotten it. Two kingdoms, properly distinguished, is not Radical Two Kingdoms. The civil sword is God's. It is not the pope's, and it is not nobody's.

John 6:15 is the gospel's own comment on Christian nationalism as a method. They would take Him by force to make Him a king, and He departed. The crown comes at the right hand, not from a crowd with a program. Render to Caesar what is Caesar's. Do not let a pontiff collect it in Christ's name.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin temporalis, of time; Greek basileia (G932), kingdom; kosmos (G2889), this world; kōsar, Caesar.

Greek apodote ta Kaisaros Kaisari (G591) — render the things of Caesar to Caesar; Matthew 22:21.

Usage

"“My kingdom is not of this world” — if it were, the servants would fight."

"“Render therefore unto Caesar” — and unto God the things that are God's, not Peter's successor's."

"“Take him by force, to make him a king” — and He departed."
